input:
Feedback control is an approach in which a process variable is held at a desired set value by continuously measuring the variable and then adjusting a flow in response to that measurement. In a level loop on a process vessel, the variable of interest is the liquid level, and the loop passes through the sensor, the controller and the final element, with the sign of the feedback determining how the loop behaves.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and converts that measurement into a signal that can be used by the rest of the loop. The measurement must genuinely represent the level in the part of the vessel the control is responsible for, and it must move when the level moves; if the sensor reads a stagnant tapping or a coated probe, it reports a level that the vessel does not really have, and every other part of the loop then acts on that false value.

The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set value. The difference between the measurement and the set value is the error, and the controller forms its output from the error, indicating how much correction is required and in which direction. The controller itself does not move anything in the process; its output is an instruction passed to the final element.

The final element carries out the instruction. In a level loop, the final element is commonly a control valve on the outlet line or on the inlet line, and it changes the flow through the vessel, which in turn changes the rate at which the level rises or falls. The level itself responds through the inventory in the vessel, because any flow imbalance integrates into a change in level.

Finally, the sign of the feedback is negative in a properly working level loop. When the level is above the set value, the loop produces an action that brings the level down, and when the level is below the set value, it produces an action that raises it, so the response always opposes the disturbance that created it. With the opposite sign, a rising level would trigger action that raises the level even further, and the loop would drive the vessel either to empty or to overflow.

The final element carries out the instruction. The level responds through the inventory in the vessel: a flow imbalance integrates into a level change, and the loop acts on that change through the sensor.
